name: The Sun (Sol)
summary: The gravitational center of our planetary system, fusing 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second in its core.

name: Mercury
summary: The smallest and innermost planet, characterized by a cratered silicate crust and an unusually large metallic iron core.

name: Venus
summary: Earth's sister world under a runaway greenhouse effect, blanketed by opaque sulfuric acid clouds and extreme atmospheric pressures.

name: Earth & Moon
summary: Only known celestial body hosting surface liquid water and an active nitrogen-oxygen biosphere, stabilized by its large lunar companion.

name: Mars
summary: A cold, iron oxide-rich desert world possessing the solar system's largest volcano (Olympus Mons) and evidence of ancient lacustrine environments.

name: Ceres
summary: The largest object in the main asteroid belt, containing roughly one-third of its total mass, featuring subsurface water ice and bright sodium carbonate salt deposits in Occator Crater.

name: Jupiter
summary: The dominant planetary mass of the solar system, featuring alternating ammonia cloud bands, persistent anticyclones, and 95 known moons.

name: Saturn
summary: Distinguished by an expansive, highly reflective ring system of water ice particles and shepherd moons spanning up to 282,000 km.

name: Uranus
summary: An ice giant world with a dynamic methane atmosphere and an extreme 97.8° axial tilt that causes retrograde, on-its-side rotation.

name: Neptune
summary: The outermost major planet, driven by supersonic atmospheric zonal winds reaching up to 2,100 km/h and high-altitude methane cirrus clouds.

name: Pluto & Charon
summary: A complex frozen world in an eccentric 2:3 orbital resonance with Neptune, featuring a vast nitrogen-ice glacier basin (Sputnik Planitia) and mountains of water ice.

name: Halley's Comet (1P/Halley)
summary: The most famous periodic retrograde comet, originating from the Kuiper/Oort reservoir and returning to perihelion every 75–76 years.

name: Voyager 1 Interstellar Probe
summary: Launched in 1977, it became the first human-made object to cross the heliopause (August 2012) and directly sample the local interstellar medium.

scientific_details.payload: The Golden Record, magnetometer, cosmic ray sensors

name: Sedna (90377 Sedna)
summary: An extremely distant, reddened planetoid with an orbital period of roughly 11,400 years, providing critical kinematic clues about potential undiscovered outer solar system masses.

name: Oort Cloud Reservoir
summary: A vast spherical swarm of volatile-rich icy planetesimals marking the outer gravitational frontier of Sol.

scientific_details.composition: Water ice, methane, ammonia, carbon monoxide

name: Alpha Centauri System
summary: Our nearest stellar neighbors, consisting of binary pair Rigil Kentaurus (G2V) and Toliman (K1V), orbited distantly by Proxima Centauri.

scientific_details.exoplanets: Proxima b, Proxima c, Proxima d

name: Barnard's Star
summary: An ancient, low-mass red dwarf exhibiting the largest known proper motion of any star relative to the Sun (10.3 arcseconds per year).

name: Sirius (The Dog Star)
summary: The brightest apparent star in Earth's night sky, paired with 'the Pup', a dense degenerate carbon-oxygen white dwarf.

name: TRAPPIST-1 System
summary: An ultra-cool red dwarf harboring seven temperate, Earth-sized terrestrial planets in tight Laplace orbital resonance, three of which lie inside the liquid water habitable zone.

scientific_details.confirmed_planets: 7 (b, c, d, e, f, g, h)

name: Vega (Alpha Lyrae)
summary: A luminous, rapid rotator bulging significantly at its equator, surrounded by a warm circumstellar dust debris ring.

name: Polaris (North Star)
summary: The Northern Celestial Pole star, an evolved yellow supergiant pulsating with a 4-day period that serves as an essential cosmic distance ladder benchmark.

name: Pleiades (Seven Sisters)
summary: An open cluster of mid-B type hot blue stars moving through an interstellar dust cloud, illuminating a faint reflection nebulosity.

name: Betelgeuse (Alpha Orionis)
summary: A pulsating red supergiant near the end of its stellar evolution, destined to undergo core-collapse into a Type II supernova.

name: Orion Nebula (M42 / NGC 1976)
summary: The nearest massive star-forming region to Earth, energized by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the nascent O and B stars of the Trapezium Cluster.

name: Crab Nebula & Pulsar (M1)
summary: The expanding gaseous debris of the core-collapse supernova observed in 1054 CE, energized by a central neutron star spinning 30 times per second.

name: Sagittarius A*
summary: The 4-million-solar-mass gravitational anchor at the nucleus of the Milky Way, shadowed by an intensely sheared synchrotron accretion flow.

name: Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC)
summary: The most massive satellite galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, housing the Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus)—the most active starburst nursery in the entire Local Group.

name: Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC)
summary: A dwarf irregular satellite companion linked to the LMC by the Magellanic Bridge, displaying low metallicity and tidal distortion.

scientific_details.gas_fraction: Extremely high neutral hydrogen (H I) content

name: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
summary: The largest galaxy in our Local Group, containing roughly one trillion stars and currently approaching the Milky Way at 110 km/s.

name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
summary: The third-largest member of the Local Group, possessing pristine, unbarred spiral arms and an intense giant H II starburst complex (NGC 604).

name: Centaurus A (NGC 5128)
type: Active Starburst Lenticular Galaxy / Radio Galaxy
summary: One of the closest radio galaxies to Earth, bisected by a chaotic dust lane resulting from a past galactic merger and venting relativistic plasma jets.

scientific_details.emission: Intense synchrotron radio and gamma-ray lobes

name: Virgo Supercluster Hub
summary: A massive gravitational gathering of thousands of galaxies, within which the Local Group occupies a small outer filament.

name: The Great Attractor (Norma Cluster Core)
summary: A massive gravitational overdensity at the center of the Laniakea Supercluster, pulling the Milky Way and hundreds of thousands of galaxies at millions of km/h.

scientific_details.location: Zone of Avoidance (obscured by Milky Way plane)

name: The Boötes Supervoid
summary: An enormous, nearly empty spherical expanse of space spanning 330 million light-years across. Where a region this size would normally contain 10,000 galaxies, fewer than 60 exist here.

name: Shapley Supercluster Concentration
summary: The most massive gravitationally bound concentration of galaxy clusters in our local universe, creating a major gravitational tug pulling our cosmic region beyond the Great Attractor.

name: El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915)
summary: The largest, hottest, and most massive merging galaxy cluster observed in the distant universe, consisting of two subclusters colliding at millions of kilometers per hour.

name: SMACS J0723.3-7327
summary: A colossal foreground galaxy cluster that acts as a natural cosmic telescope, bending and magnifying light from galaxies over 13 billion light years away.

scientific_details.lens_phenomenon: Relativistic Einstein rings and tangential arcs

name: GN-z11 Primordial Galaxy
summary: One of the most distant known galaxies, observed just 400 million years after the Big Bang. Intensely luminous and compact, its light is heavily redshifted into the infrared spectrum.

name: Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)
summary: The surface of last scattering: relic thermal radiation emitted 380,000 years after the Big Bang, marking the absolute visual edge of the observable universe.
